title: Napoleon's strategy at Ulm
subject: histoire
description: In October 1805, Napoleon surrounded and captured **60,000 Austrians** in two weeks, with almost no major battle. Ulm showed the power of speed.

hero.hook: In two weeks, Napoleon captured a whole army without ever fighting the big battle.

blocks.text: In October **1805**, **Napoleon Bonaparte** had been Emperor of the French for less than a year. In two weeks he pulled off something rare: he surrounded and captured an Austrian army of about **60,000 troops**, with almost no pitched battle.
The campaign turned on **Ulm**, a fortified town in southern Germany on the Danube. Napoleon proved there that a war can be won by speed and secrecy, not only by a frontal clash.

England paid for an alliance against France: the **Third Coalition**. It brought together the Austria of Emperor **Francis II** and the Russia of Tsar **Alexander I**. But Austria did not wait for the Russians. General **Karl Mack**, who commanded the Austrian army, pushed about **70,000 troops** as far as Ulm. He thought the place could not be taken.

blocks.caption: Napoleon Bonaparte, Emperor for less than a year in 1805

blocks.text: The Russian army used the Julian calendar, **12 days** behind the Austrian one. The confusion delayed the reinforcements further and left Mack isolated at Ulm.

Mack expected the French from the west, out of the [[Black Forest]], a range of hills in southwestern Germany. He neglected his flanks and his rear. Meanwhile the Russians under General **Kutuzov** were still far to the east.

Napoleon dropped the idea of invading England, at least for a while. He swung his [[Grande Armée]] toward Germany. His trump card was the [[Napoleonic Army Corps]]. Each corps was a small self-contained army, with its own infantry, cavalry, and guns. Seven of them marched along parallel roads.

On **September 25**, about **210,000 troops** crossed the Rhine. Marshal **Murat**, Napoleon's brother-in-law and his cavalry commander, held Mack's attention in the west. Meanwhile other marshals (Bernadotte, Davout, Soult, Ney, Lannes) swung around Ulm from the north, covering nearly **30 km a day**.
On **October 7**, the French crossed the Danube behind Mack. He was cut off from Vienna, the Austrian capital, and from the Russians. The trap at Ulm had closed.

sections.title: An army that surrenders without a battle

blocks.text: Mack tried to break out, notably at **Elchingen**, a nearby village. Marshal **Ney** took the heights there. On **October 17, 1805**, Mack surrendered: **27,000** soldiers laid down their arms on the spot. Across the whole campaign, Austria lost about **60,000 troops**.

blocks.caption: The surrender of Ulm: an army captured with almost no decisive battle

blocks.text: After the surrender, Napoleon invited the Austrian officers to dinner. Mack introduced himself: “Here is the unfortunate Mack.” The Emperor handed him back his sword.

It was a victory of legs as much as of courage. But that same week, at the [[Battle of Trafalgar]], off the Spanish coast, the British admiral Nelson destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet. Napoleon ruled the continent. England kept the sea.

The road to **Vienna** lay open. The French entered the city on **November 13**. Then, on **December 2, 1805**, at **Austerlitz** (in what is now the Czech Republic), Napoleon beat the Austrians and the Russians. Ulm became a model: paralyze the enemy before you strike him. To try to ruin England another way, Napoleon would soon invent the [[Continental System]], which banned European trade with London.

blocks.text: In October **1805**, Napoleon captured **60,000** Austrians at Ulm with almost no decisive battle: speed and maneuver counted for as much as the frontal clash.
